15 State Priority and Perturbation Sensitivity 15.1 Perturbation Priority 15.2 Rare Cell Detection 15.3 The Workflow Shell 15.4 The AI Layer: run_rare_cell_detection 15.5 What Fits Nearby 15.6 Current Recommendation 15.7 What Is Not Here Yet

15 State Priority and Perturbation Sensitivity After clustering, annotation, and trajectory analysis, one question still remains: which states actually respond to the perturbation, and which states are so small that the clustering averaged them away? These are two different questions with two different methods, and this mainline exists to keep them apart. Perturbation priority asks which cell types change most between conditions. It is a sensitivity ranking, not an abundance test. sclet answers it with RunPerturbationPriority(), a wrapper around Augur. Rare cell detection asks which small populations did the clustering miss or bury. It is a density analysis on the embedding, not a model of condition. sclet answers it with RunRareCellDetection(). Both write into the same state layer as every other mainline, so both can be inspected, replayed, and cited. RunStatePriorityWorkflow() is the shell that runs them as one record when you want the pair. 15.1 Perturbation Priority Augur trains a classifier per cell type to predict the experimental condition from expression, then scores each cell type by its cross-validated AUC. A cell type whose identity is barely affected by the treatment is hard to classify and scores near 0.5; a cell type that reorganizes strongly scores near 1. The ranking is therefore a ranking of transcriptional responsiveness, which is not the same thing as effect size, and not the same thing as abundance. 15.1.1 What the object has to satisfy RunPerturbationPriority() validates before it computes, and each check corresponds to a real class of mistake: condition_col must name a colData column with at least two distinct levels. A single-level column means there is nothing to classify. group_col must name a colData column. NULL falls back to ActiveIdent(sce), and the special value "colLabels" is resolved from SingleCellExperiment::colLabels() so a clustering written into colLabels can be used without copying it into a new column first. The expression source is resolved with sclet_resolve_expression_source(..., prefer_nonscaled = TRUE, fallback_layers = c("logcounts")): a scaled layer is explicitly avoided, because a classifier fitted on z-scores is a classifier fitted on a different quantity per gene. library(sclet) # Two conditions, and a cluster column. pbmc$condition <- ifelse(seq_len(ncol(pbmc)) %% 2 == 0, "treated", "control") unique(pbmc$condition) ## [1] "control" "treated" # The two columns the run will read. c(condition = "condition", group = "colLabels") ## condition group ## "condition" "colLabels" The condition column here is synthetic — it alternates by cell index and carries no biology. That is deliberate: the point of this section is the mechanics of the ranking, and a real design needs real replicates (see Current Recommendation for what a real design has to look like). Any AUC this produces is a property of the random split, not a discovery. 15.1.2 The direct call pbmc <- RunPerturbationPriority( pbmc, condition_col = "condition", group_col = "colLabels", name = "augur_main" ) The result is stored twice, deliberately, because the two copies serve different readers: the analysis layer under the key "augur", read by get_perturbation_priority(). This is the user-facing copy and includes the raw Augur result list. the typed state layer as a record of type "priority" with method = "Augur", which carries the inputs (condition_col, group_col, assay, layer), the AUC table, and the extra arguments passed through .... Everything passed in ... is forwarded to Augur::calculate_auc(), so tuning the classifier happens through the usual Augur arguments rather than through new sclet parameters. 15.1.3 Reading the result back has_perturbation_priority(pbmc) ## [1] TRUE # The whole record, or one element of it. head(get_perturbation_priority(pbmc, element = "AUC")) ## # A tibble: 6 × 2 ## cell_type auc ## <chr> <dbl> ## 1 Naive CD4+ T 0.532 ## 2 B 0.516 ## 3 Stress Response / Malignant Cells 0.506 ## 4 NK 0.495 ## 5 CD14+ Mono 0.492 ## 6 CD8+ T 0.483 # The ranking as a bar chart (top 20 by AUC). plot_perturbation_ranking(pbmc) has_perturbation_priority() is worth calling first in any script that reads the record: it returns FALSE rather than erroring on an object where Augur never ran, which keeps a downstream report from failing on a partially analysed object. Note that get_perturbation_priority() reads the analysis record ("augur"), not the typed state record. get_perturbation() is the CellOracle accessor and reads a different state type, so on an object where only Augur has run it returns NULL — the two names are easy to confuse and they do not overlap. 15.2 Rare Cell Detection RunRareCellDetection(method = "density") labels small populations directly on the kNN graph of a reduction. It needs no Python, no annotation reference, and no condition labels — only BiocNeighbors (already a sclet dependency) and a PCA. The algorithm: Build the kNN graph on the chosen dimensions and compute each cell’s mutual connectivity Q: the fraction of its k neighbours that list it as a neighbour too. Q is high where the graph is locally dense. Seed on local maxima — a cell becomes a seed when its Q exceeds the median Q of its own neighbours and clears q_threshold. Adjacent seeds are merged through their mutual kNN links before anything propagates, because two adjacent dense cells belong to one density peak. Propagate labels outward for five iterations, then dissolve any group smaller than min_cluster_size into its densest neighbouring group. Flag every group with at most rare_threshold cells as rare. Both the seeding rule and the dissolution step are the results of a measured failure, and the chapter should say so plainly. The first version of this seeding rule treated every cell above q_threshold as its own seed, and on PBMC 3k that produced 2419 “populations” for 2700 cells, 75% of them one cell. A one-cell population is where a cell happened to sit, not a population. The current rule — local maximum, merge adjacent seeds, dissolve what remains below min_cluster_size — is what makes the label column interpretable. The first run is on the shared pbmc object, because that is the object every chapter uses: library(sclet) # PCA already exists on pbmc from the core workflow. rare_demo <- RunRareCellDetection( pbmc, method = "density", reduction = "PCA", dims = 1:10, k = 20, q_threshold = 0.25, rare_threshold = 10, name = "density_demo" ) rare_info <- get_rare_cells(rare_demo) c(n_clusters = rare_info$n_clusters, n_rare_clusters = rare_info$n_rare_clusters) ## n_clusters n_rare_clusters ## 4 0 That run is a negative result, and it is a useful one: the PBMC 3k embedding is a small number of broad blobs, so the density rule consolidates everything and n_rare_clusters comes back 0. Nothing is wrong with the function — it is reporting that the embedding has no small isolated peak. On a real dataset this is the answer that tells you not to spend time on a follow-up. To see the positive case, and to test the AI layer’s evidence grading, the chapter builds a small object with a population the clustering does separate. The fixture is 409 cells, three hundred genes, and a nine-cell block with twenty of its own up-regulated genes — small enough to render fast, structured enough that “rare population” means something: set.seed(7) n_genes <- 300 n_main <- 400 n_rare <- 9 rare_columns <- n_main + seq_len(n_rare) fixture_counts <- matrix( rpois(n_genes * (n_main + n_rare), lambda = 3), nrow = n_genes, dimnames = list(paste0("gene_", seq_len(n_genes)), paste0("cell_", seq_len(n_main + n_rare)))) # The rare block is marked by genes the rest of the object does not express. fixture_counts[seq_len(20), rare_columns] <- fixture_counts[seq_len(20), rare_columns] + 120 fixture <- SingleCellExperiment(list(counts = fixture_counts)) fixture <- NormalizeData(fixture) fixture <- FindVariableFeatures(fixture, nfeatures = 150) fixture <- RunPCA(fixture, ncomponents = 10) fixture <- FindNeighbors(fixture, dims = 1:10) fixture <- FindClusters(fixture, resolution = 0.5) # The clustering already separates the small block. table(SingleCellExperiment::colLabels(fixture)) ## ## 1 2 ## 400 9 # k = 10 rather than the default 20: with k = 20 the 9-cell block's neighbours # reach into the main blob and the group is dissolved. This is a property of # small populations in general, not of the fixture -- k has to be small enough # that a rare cell's neighbourhood stays inside the rare population. fixture <- RunRareCellDetection( fixture, method = "density", reduction = "PCA", dims = 1:10, k = 10, rare_threshold = 10, min_cluster_size = 2L, name = "rareq" ) fixture_counts_by_group <- table(fixture$rare_cluster) fixture_counts_by_group ## ## 1 2 ## 400 9 fixture_info <- get_rare_cells(fixture) c(n_clusters = fixture_info$n_clusters, n_rare_clusters = fixture_info$n_rare_clusters) ## n_clusters n_rare_clusters ## 2 1 The label column and the recorded counts agree: two groups, one of them the nine-cell population, which rare_threshold = 10 flags as rare. 15.3 The Workflow Shell RunStatePriorityWorkflow() runs either or both analyses and records them as one mainline record pointing at the component ids: pbmc <- RunStatePriorityWorkflow( pbmc, condition_col = "condition", group_col = "colLabels", run_perturbation_priority = TRUE, run_rare_cell_detection = TRUE, name = "state_priority_main" ) The shell refuses an empty request (needs at least one prioritization task enabled) rather than writing a workflow record that describes nothing. Note one asymmetry that is easy to trip over: the shell passes its own name-derived ids to the components (<name>_priority, <name>_rare) and forwards ... to those components. The rare-cell component is called with its defaults only, so reduction, dims and k for rare detection are not configurable through this shell — call RunRareCellDetection() directly when you need to change them. 15.4 The AI Layer: run_rare_cell_detection The AI action layer exposes run_rare_cell_detection, which wraps RunRareCellDetection() and then writes one evidence node per small population. The action’s prerequisite is narrow and worth knowing: it needs the named reduction to exist (either on the object or as a planned reduction earlier in the same plan) and BiocNeighbors to be installed. It does not require condition labels — rare cell detection is not a condition analysis. 15.4.1 The ordering rule that costs a run to learn This is the single most important practical fact about the action, and it is in AGENTS.md because it was measured on real billed runs: run_de_test must come before run_rare_cell_detection in the plan. The reason is in how evidence is graded. Each rare population’s evidence node is graded by n_independent_signals — the number of independent signal classes informative for that population at the moment the action runs. Four classes are considered: QC metrics, doublet calls, an attributable marker test, and sample replication. Cluster size alone is never a signal. If the marker test has not run yet, the marker class is unavailable, and on an object with no QC columns, no scDblFinder calls and no sample column either, zero signal classes are available. The action then records nothing at all and stamps a no_evidence_recorded note on the returned object. A plan can still complete every step, the object still gains a rare_cluster column, and the ledger holds no evidence — the “message and artifact disagree” shape of failure that a plan validator cannot see, because ordering markers after rare detection is not invalid, only useless. The two runs below are the same fixture, same parameters, same population. The only difference is whether the marker test ran first: registry <- AIDefaultExecutionRegistry(fixture, include = "all") # --- Ordering A: rare detection on an object with no marker test. --- rare_first <- registry$run_rare_cell_detection$handler(fixture, list(reduction = "PCA", dims = 1:10, k = 10, rare_threshold = 10, min_cluster_size = 2L, name = "rareq_A")) # --- Ordering B: marker test first, then rare detection. --- de_first <- RunDEtest(fixture, name = "findallmarkers") de_first <- registry$run_rare_cell_detection$handler(de_first, list(reduction = "PCA", dims = 1:10, k = 10, rare_threshold = 10, min_cluster_size = 2L, name = "rareq_B")) # Evidence nodes recorded under each ordering. c(rare_first = length(sclet:::sclet_ai_evidence_get_all(rare_first)), de_first = length(sclet:::sclet_ai_evidence_get_all(de_first))) ## rare_first de_first ## 0 1 Ordering A records nothing for the nine-cell group. Ordering B records one node, and its fields explain why the grade is what it is: node <- sclet:::sclet_ai_evidence_get_all(de_first)[[1]] unlist(node$values)[c("population_label", "population_size", "n_independent_signals", "marker_available", "sample_replication_available", "low_confidence")] ## population_label population_size ## "group_2" "9" ## n_independent_signals marker_available ## "1" "TRUE" ## sample_replication_available low_confidence ## "FALSE" "TRUE" node$claim_level ## [1] "associated" One signal class is available — the marker test — so the claim is levelled "associated" and the node is marked low_confidence = TRUE. Adding sample replication or doublet calls would raise it to "consistent_with". The same grading is available directly, without going through the action, which is the call to make when you want to know before relying on a rare population how much support it would have: # Marker test first: an all-cluster marker run records markers per cluster, so # each population can then be credited individually. signals <- summarize_small_cluster_evidence(de_first, cluster = "rare_cluster", size_threshold = 10) unlist(signals$independent_signals$marker)[c("available", "n_significant_up_genes")] ## available n_significant_up_genes ## 1 20 # The count the evidence grade is built from. signals$n_independent_signals_available ## [1] 1 15.4.2 Why the whole thing is not executed through a plan Everything above calls the registered handler directly. The full path — AIPlanAnalysis() proposing a plan, ValidateAIPlan() approving it, ExecuteAIPlan() running it — is a billed model call, so it runs only on a machine with a provider configured (SCLET_BOOKDOWN_EVAL_AI=1). The handler is the layer that writes the evidence, so calling it directly tests the same ordering rule without a model in the middle. plan <- AIPlanAnalysis(fixture, goal = "find rare populations and support them with marker evidence") # What the planner proposed, in order. This is the part that varies. vapply(plan$actions, function(step) step$action, character(1)) ## [1] "run_de_test" "run_rare_cell_detection" # Three arguments are easy to get wrong here and none of them fails loudly: # validation takes the plan FIRST, the token lives on the validation object, # and `dry_run` defaults to TRUE -- omit it and the "execution" is a preview # that reports `status = "dry_run"` with no evidence, which reads exactly like # a plan that ran and found nothing. validation <- ValidateAIPlan(plan, object = fixture, registry = registry) if (isTRUE(validation$valid)) { out <- ExecuteAIPlan(fixture, plan, registry, validation = validation, dry_run = FALSE, confirmation = validation$confirmation_token) evidence <- sclet:::sclet_ai_evidence_get_all(out$object) c(status = out$status, steps = length(out$results), evidence_nodes = length(evidence)) } else { # Refused before anything ran. This is the common outcome on this object, # and the reason is the ordering rule above. validation$errors } ## status steps evidence_nodes ## "completed" "2" "1" Three outcomes are all reachable here, and telling them apart is the skill this section is teaching: refused (validation$valid is FALSE, nothing runs): the plan is illegal for this object. The most likely reason on fixture is ordering — it has already been through RunRareCellDetection(), which leaves a single identity group (the rare labels live in their own column, not in colLabels), so a marker test placed after the detection has no second group to test against and fails its prerequisite. completed — every step ran. The evidence count says whether any of them left something citable; 0 is a real answer, not an error. failed — the plan was legal and a step still failed at run time. The steps before it may have recorded evidence, so evidence_nodes can be non-zero on a failed execution. Nothing is rolled back. Which one you get changes between runs, because the planner is a language model and not a fixed recipe. So the chunk above reports the outcome it got instead of asserting the outcome it should have got — and that is the honest shape of AI-assisted analysis. The engine’s guarantee is narrow and worth stating precisely: the model proposes an order, the engine decides whether that order is legal, and neither of them promises that a legal order was a useful one. 15.5 What Fits Nearby Before this chapter: the core workflow for clustering, and reference mapping if you want group_col to hold cell types rather than cluster codes. Augur’s ranking is only as interpretable as its groups. Alongside this chapter: the Milo chapter answers the abundance question — did this neighbourhood change its cell count between conditions — where Augur answers the transcriptional question. A cell type can be highly responsive and unchanged in abundance, and the reverse, so the two tables are read together, not instead of each other. After this chapter: communication and spatial analysis can test whether the top-ranked states are also the ones whose signalling or location changed. 15.6 Current Recommendation The recommendation has boundaries, because both methods are easy to over-read: Use RunPerturbationPriority() when the question is “which of my annotated cell types respond transcriptionally to the perturbation”, you have at least two conditions with reasonable cell numbers per (cell type × condition) cell, and you are willing to install Augur from GitHub. Treat the AUC as an ordinal ranking with a null of 0.5, not as an effect size, and check that the top-ranked type is not simply the one with the most cells. Do not use it when you have one sample per condition. Augur’s cross-validation operates within the pooled cells and does not model donor-level correlation, so a per-donor batch effect can be read as responsiveness. Milo’s mixed model (the Milo chapter) is the right tool for a sample-level design. Use RunRareCellDetection(method = "density") when you suspect a small population was averaged into a larger cluster, and you want a cheap, deterministic, annotation-free labelling of candidate small populations on the embedding. It is suitable as a screening step: it tells you where to look. Do not use it as evidence that a population is real. The label column is a density artefact detector, not a biological claim. A small population needs independent support — markers, doublet scores, QC behaviour, and replication across samples — which is exactly what the AI layer’s evidence grading encodes, and exactly why run_de_test has to run first. On the PBMC demo object the run consolidates everything and reports n_rare_clusters = 0: that is the method working. When you want both, call RunStatePriorityWorkflow() with both flags for the convenience of one record, but call RunRareCellDetection() directly if you need to change reduction, dims, k, or min_cluster_size — the shell does not forward those. 15.7 What Is Not Here Yet No sample-level recombination for Augur. RunPerturbationPriority() passes the pooled expression matrix to Augur::calculate_auc(). There is no per-donor cross-validation and no random effect, so a design with one sample per condition is not supported — use Milo. No scCODA, no composition model of any kind. sclet has no Bayesian compositional analysis for condition effects on cluster proportions. Milo covers neighbourhood abundance; scCODA-style compositional modelling of the cluster table does not exist here. No CellOracle-level in-silico perturbation here. There is RunInSilicoPerturbation() in the spatial mainline, which is a different thing: a GRN-based simulation. It is not connected to the priority ranking, and nothing lets you take “cell type 3 is the most responsive” and simulate a knockout in it in one call. No second prioritization backend. RunStatePriorityWorkflow() dispatches only Augur. The documentation of the shell says other prioritization modules “will be added as backends mature”; none is wired today, so a state-priority record’s only possible component is perturbation_priority and/or rare_cells. No rare-cell-evidence action other than the density method. RunRareCellDetection() accepts method = c("density") only. There is no UMAP-density variant, no label-propagation-from-markers variant, and no supervised rare-cell classifier. The rare-cell evidence is not a p-value. Nothing here computes significance for a rare population. The evidence nodes record how many independent signal classes support the population and at what claim level, which is a calibration of confidence, not a test.

16 Spatial Context and Niche Analysis 16.1 Spatial Mainline Workflow 16.2 High-Resolution Spatial Deconvolution: Cell2location 16.3 Spatial Colocalization with SVP 16.4 Spatial Niche Detection with SVP LISA 16.5 Inspecting Spatial Results Across Layers 16.6 In-Silico Gene Perturbation: CellOracle

16 Spatial Context and Niche Analysis This mainline extends the analysis map from dissociated single cells back into tissue context. The user question is no longer only which states exist, but where they sit, which compositions change across space, and how niche structure constrains interpretation. sclet now provides RunSpatialWorkflow() as the semantic shell, with RunSpatialDeconvolution() as the primary backend and RunSpatialColocalization() and RunSpatialNiche() reserved for future integration. All spatial functions now follow the same state contract as other sclet modules: each runs records a name identifier, writes into the typed state record layer, and logs the command for downstream provenance tracking. 16.1 Spatial Mainline Workflow The simplest entry point is the workflow shell. It dispatches deconvolution through cell2location and reserves colocalization and niche slots. library(sclet) # sce_spatial: spatial SingleCellExperiment with 'counts' assay # sce_ref: reference scRNA-seq SCE with cell type labels sce_spatial <- RunSpatialWorkflow( sce_spatial, sce_ref = sce_ref, ref_group_key = "cell_type", run_deconvolution = TRUE, name = "my_spatial_analysis" ) # Check the active spatial state has_spatial(sce_spatial) get_spatial(sce_spatial) 16.2 High-Resolution Spatial Deconvolution: Cell2location cell2location is widely recognized as the “gold standard” for spatial deconvolution. It uses a negative binomial regression model to map scRNA-seq reference data onto spatial spots, inferring the true absolute abundance of each cell type within a given location. In sclet, this complex Bayesian inference is simplified into a single line of code: To run this locally, the minimum prerequisites are a spatial object with a counts assay, a reference SCE with the same gene space, and a biologically meaningful cell-type column in colData(sce_ref). The name parameter lets you tag each run so that multiple deconvolution results can coexist in the same object. library(sclet) # Assume 'sce_spatial' is your spatial transcriptomics object, # and 'sce_ref' is your single-cell reference object with a "cell_type" column. sce_spatial <- RunSpatialDeconvolution( sce_spatial, sce_ref, ref_group_key = "cell_type", max_epochs = 50, name = "my_deconv" ) Under the Hood: The function trains the model through the basilisk environment. device = "cuda" selects sclet’s GPU environment when one is available; the default is "cpu" — see the integration chapter. Once complete, the predicted abundances for each cell type are directly appended to colData(sce_spatial), and the spatial state is activated through sclet_set_analysis_state(). Each run is also logged via sclet_log_command(), so CommandLog(sce_spatial) will show the parameters and timestamp. You can immediately use spatial plotting functions to visualize the distribution of specific cell types across the tissue slice. 16.3 Spatial Colocalization with SVP RunSpatialColocalization() uses the SVP package’s global bivariate spatial autocorrelation (runGLOBALBV()) to test whether pairs of features tend to co-occur in the same spatial regions. The cached object below already contains the precomputed result, so bookdown only reads the saved object. spe <- readRDS("data/visium-dlpfc-sub.rds") top_features <- S4Vectors::metadata(spe)$sclet_bookdown_cache$top_features top_features ## [1] "ENSG00000186468" "ENSG00000228253" "ENSG00000157152" ## [4] "ENSG00000133083" "ENSG00000058404" has_colocalization(spe) ## [1] FALSE 16.4 Spatial Niche Detection with SVP LISA RunSpatialNiche() uses SVP’s Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA). The cached object below already contains the precomputed LISA result. has_spatial_niche(spe) ## [1] FALSE 16.5 Inspecting Spatial Results Across Layers Because all spatial functions now register through the unified state layer, a single accessor pattern works for deconvolution, colocalization, and niche results alike. When you keep multiple spatial records, use id to address a specific one. # The default spatial record (active state) has_spatial(sce) get_spatial(sce, element = "columns") # A specific spatial record by id get_spatial(sce, id = "my_deconv") # Colocalization and niche records have their own accessors has_colocalization(sce) get_colocalization(sce, element = "status") has_spatial_niche(sce) 16.6 In-Silico Gene Perturbation: CellOracle Differential expression tells you “what changed,” SCENIC tells you “who is controlling,” but CellOracle allows you to conduct thought experiments (In-silico Perturbation). Imagine asking: If I knockout the GATA2 gene in hematopoietic stem cells, how will their developmental trajectory shift? Performing this in vitro is costly and time-consuming. In sclet, it takes only a few minutes of simulation. This simulation only makes sense after you have already constructed a compatible GRN prior and a dimensional representation that captures the state manifold you want to perturb. # Assume 'sce' has already been processed through SCENIC (to obtain a GRN), # has an active dimensional reduction space, and you have exported a base GRN file. base_grn_path <- "path/to/celloracle_base_grn.csv" sce <- RunInSilicoPerturbation( sce, target_gene = "GATA2", perturbation_value = 0.0, # Simulate a full knockout base_grn_path = base_grn_path, cluster_key = "cell_type", reduction = "PCA" ) # Inspect the perturbation state get_perturbation(sce) The Impact: The inferred cellular shift vectors are carefully recorded. When combined with streamplots or vector field visualizations, you can intuitively observe on the UMAP space: in a parallel universe without GATA2, which terminal state are these cells “fleeing” from, and which incorrect lineage are they “rushing” toward?

17 Multimodal Expansion 17.1 The Two States: Attached and Registered 17.2 Detecting and Registering 17.3 One-Step Registration 17.4 The AI Layer 17.5 What Is Not Here Yet 17.6 What to Do Today

17 Multimodal Expansion Most sclet chapters assume one assay on one object. Real CITE-seq and multiome datasets carry a second modality — antibody counts (ADT) or chromatin accessibility (ATAC) — that has the same cells as the RNA assay but a different feature space. This chapter covers what sclet actually does with that second modality today. The answer is short and specific. sclet implements the object contract for multimodal data: it detects a modality, registers it as a typed state record, and exposes both the object layer and the AI layer to code that can reason about a modality existing. It does not implement modality analysis: there is no ADT clustering, no ATAC peak calling, no cross-modality integration, and no multiome preprocessing. The next section shows the contract, and What Is Not Here Yet lists exactly what is missing and why it is not there. 17.1 The Two States: Attached and Registered The chapter only makes sense if one distinction is kept sharp, because the AI layer and the diagnostic layer both depend on it: Attached: an altExp named "ADT" or "ATAC" exists on the object. The data is present. has_multimodal_adt() / has_multimodal_atac() answer this. Registered: a multimodal analysis-state record exists for that modality, so the mainline can talk about it without reaching into object internals. register_multimodal_adt() / register_multimodal_atac() write that record. Registration records dimensions and nothing else. It performs no integration, no batch correction, no normalization and no modality-specific analysis. Every function in this chapter is written to respect that: the records below store n_features and n_cells of the stored altExp, which describes how large the modality is, not how informative it is. 17.2 Detecting and Registering The two helpers are thin, and that is the point: they are the only place where sclet decides whether a modality “exists”. library(sclet) # The PBMC demo object carries a single RNA assay, so both helpers are FALSE. c(adt = has_multimodal_adt(pbmc), atac = has_multimodal_atac(pbmc)) ## adt atac ## FALSE FALSE Attaching a modality is an ordinary SingleCellExperiment operation. sclet deliberately does not wrap it, because the data is not sclet’s to read: # `pbmc` has no colnames, so index by position rather than by name: a character # subset against a NULL vector silently selects zero cells. cell_index <- seq_len(40) demo_multimodal <- pbmc[, cell_index] # Give the subset real cell names and build the altExp from THOSE, so the two # layers agree on which cell is which. An altExp whose colnames differ from its # parent's is not a modality of that object: `altExp<-` warns today # ("'colnames(value)' are not the same as 'colnames(x)'") and the message says # it will become an error in the next Bioconductor release (measured # 2026-10-21). cell_ids <- paste0("cell_", cell_index) colnames(demo_multimodal) <- cell_ids altExp(demo_multimodal, "ADT") <- multimodal_alt(cell_ids, prefix = "ADT_feature_") has_multimodal_adt(demo_multimodal) ## [1] TRUE SingleCellExperiment::altExpNames(demo_multimodal) ## [1] "ADT" Registration is the only step that touches the state layer. It fails loudly on an object that does not carry the modality, which is the behaviour you want: silent registration of an absent modality would make the rest of the chapter lie. # Registering an absent modality is an error, not a no-op. tryCatch(register_multimodal_adt(pbmc), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)) ## [1] "altExp(sce, \"ADT\") not found. Load ADT data into the object first." demo_multimodal <- register_multimodal_adt(demo_multimodal, name = "demo_ADT") The registered record is readable through the analysis ledger, so it participates in provenance exactly like an Augur or Milo run. The ledger is the bounded view the AI layer reads, which is why it is also the right place to look as a user: # The analysis ledger groups records by state type; "multimodal" is now a key. ledger <- GetAnalysisLedger(demo_multimodal, detail = "summary") names(ledger$state_records) ## [1] "preprocess" "reduction" "graph" ## [4] "clustering" "geneset_scoring" "priority" ## [7] "rare_cells" "multimodal" # The state record says which modality was registered and by which method. record <- ledger$state_records$multimodal[[1]] record[c("id", "method")] ## $id ## [1] "demo_ADT" ## ## $method ## [1] "altExp_ADT" The stored dimensions live on the analysis layer written by the same call, not on the state record: # `unlist` because the ledger view returns the analysis as a nested list. unlist(ledger$analyses$multimodal_adt[c("id", "n_features", "n_cells")]) ## id ## "demo_ADT" ## [1] 1 17.3 One-Step Registration RunMultimodalWorkflow() is a workflow shell over the two registration calls. It detects every modality it knows about, registers each one, and then writes a single multimodal_workflow record that points at the component records. It is useful mainly as the one place that answers “what modalities does this object have, as far as sclet is concerned”. multi <- pbmc[, cell_index] colnames(multi) <- cell_ids altExp(multi, "ADT") <- multimodal_alt(cell_ids, prefix = "ADT_feature_") altExp(multi, "ATAC") <- multimodal_alt(cell_ids, n_features = 8L, prefix = "peak_") multi <- RunMultimodalWorkflow(multi, name = "demo_multi") # Two modality records plus the workflow record that points at them. names(GetAnalysisLedger(multi, detail = "summary")$state_records$multimodal) ## [1] "demo_multi_ADT" "demo_multi_ATAC" The important negative case is the demo object: with no altExps, RunMultimodalWorkflow() returns the object unchanged and says so. It does not invent a record, and it does not fail — a workflow shell that hard-errors on an RNA-only object would be hostile to the common case. unchanged <- RunMultimodalWorkflow(pbmc) identical(unchanged, pbmc) ## [1] TRUE 17.4 The AI Layer The AI layer exposes three read-only actions for multimodal data. All three are in the multimodal action group (AIDefaultExecutionRegistry(sce, include = "multimodal")), all three are read-only (mutates_object = FALSE), and none of them writes an evidence node: they report state, they do not measure anything. Action Reads Returns check_multimodal_readiness altExps + multimodal state records status, per-modality adt_available / atac_available / *_registered, workflow_record_available, questions summarize_multimodal_evidence the registered records n_modalities, modality_kinds, per-kind n_features / n_cells, fixed caveats compare_multimodal_evidence two or more registered records anonymised group_N codes plus per-code counts, or status = "not_available" All three have a prerequisite of the same shape: no multimodal state record means the action refuses. Attaching an altExp without registering it is not enough for the AI layer, which is why the previous section exists. registry <- AIDefaultExecutionRegistry(pbmc, include = "multimodal") names(registry) ## [1] "check_multimodal_readiness" ## [2] "summarize_multimodal_evidence" ## [3] "compare_multimodal_evidence" # One line of refusal, naming the missing state rather than failing. registry$check_multimodal_readiness$prerequisites(pbmc, list()) ## [1] "no_multimodal_record: no multimodal state record is available on this object; no multimodal analysis has been recorded yet." Readiness distinguishes the three interesting situations, and reports them in the questions field instead of acting on them: # 1. Attached, not registered. attached_only <- pbmc[, cell_index] colnames(attached_only) <- cell_ids altExp(attached_only, "ADT") <- multimodal_alt(cell_ids, prefix = "ADT_feature_") ready <- check_multimodal_readiness(attached_only) ready$status ## [1] "ready_for_diagnostic" ready$checks[c("adt_available", "adt_registered", "workflow_record_available")] ## $adt_available ## [1] TRUE ## ## $adt_registered ## [1] FALSE ## ## $workflow_record_available ## [1] FALSE # 2. Nothing multimodal at all. check_multimodal_readiness(pbmc)$status ## [1] "not_ready" The bounded summaries are length-limited on purpose. They return counts, booleans and the platform labels "ADT" / "ATAC" — never a feature name, an antibody name, a barcode or a per-cell value — so they can be put into a prompt without leaking the dataset. summary_of_demo <- summarize_multimodal_evidence(demo_multimodal) summary_of_demo[c("status", "n_modalities", "modality_kinds", "raw_values_included")] ## $status ## [1] "available" ## ## $n_modalities ## [1] 1 ## ## $modality_kinds ## [1] "ADT" ## ## $raw_values_included ## [1] FALSE summary_of_demo$modalities$ADT ## $n_features ## [1] 5 ## ## $n_cells ## [1] 40 ## ## $raw_values_included ## [1] FALSE # The caveats travel with the summary so no reader quotes the counts as quality. length(summary_of_demo$caveats) ## [1] 4 compare_multimodal_evidence() requires two registered modalities. This is the case that most often surprises people, and it is not a bug: # One registered modality: refusal with a reason, not a comparison of one thing. compare_multimodal_evidence(demo_multimodal)[c("status", "reason", "n_modalities")] ## $status ## [1] "not_available" ## ## $reason ## [1] "at_least_two_modalities_required" ## ## $n_modalities ## [1] 1 # Two registered modalities: comparison by anonymised code only. comparison <- compare_multimodal_evidence(multi) comparison[c("status", "n_modalities", "modality_codes")] ## $status ## [1] "available" ## ## $n_modalities ## [1] 2 ## ## $modality_codes ## [1] "group_1" "group_2" comparison$modalities ## $group_1 ## $group_1$n_features ## [1] 5 ## ## $group_1$n_cells ## [1] 40 ## ## $group_1$raw_values_included ## [1] FALSE ## ## ## $group_2 ## $group_2$n_features ## [1] 8 ## ## $group_2$n_cells ## [1] 40 ## ## $group_2$raw_values_included ## [1] FALSE Two properties of these results are deliberate and worth stating plainly. First, the comparison is over stored dimensions of different assay platforms: a modality with more features is not more informative, and nothing here ranks or prefers one. Second, the modality labels come back as group_1 / group_2 so that a summary can describe a two-modality object without naming the platform in a result that might be re-sent elsewhere. Registration is also what carries the modality into the planning context. Without a record the AI layer has no multimodal state to read, and the action catalog it sees for this object is a plain RNA catalog: multimodal_actions <- c("check_multimodal_readiness", "summarize_multimodal_evidence", "compare_multimodal_evidence") # Registered: the three multimodal actions are visible to a planner. # available_actions is a list of descriptors, so the names are pulled out. context <- sclet:::sclet_ai_context(demo_multimodal, target = "planning", detail = "summary", registry = registry) offered <- vapply(context$available_actions, function(a) a$name, character(1)) # `intersect` is ambiguous once `sclet` is attached (dplyr, GenomicRanges and # base all export one), so the base implementation is named explicitly -- # `library(conflicted)` turns the silent ambiguity into a hard error rather # than a warning. base::intersect(offered, multimodal_actions) ## [1] "check_multimodal_readiness" ## [2] "summarize_multimodal_evidence" ## [3] "compare_multimodal_evidence" # Never invented: a registry that excludes the group cannot offer them. AIDefaultExecutionRegistry(demo_multimodal, include = "read") |> names() |> base::intersect(multimodal_actions) ## character(0) 17.5 What Is Not Here Yet Everything below the object contract is absent, and it is absent because no backend has been wired in. This is the full list of what a reader would reasonably expect from a chapter titled “multimodal expansion” and will not find in sclet today: No cross-modality integration. There is no WNN, MOFA, scMoMaT, totalVI or MultiVI. register_multimodal_*() records that an ADT or ATAC altExp exists; it does not produce a joint embedding, a corrected assay, or a combined neighbour graph. Any RunIntegration() call operates on the RNA assay alone. No ADT analysis. There is no CLR normalization, no ADT-specific marker test, no ADT-based clustering, and no ADT QC beyond whatever QC you computed yourself. The ADT altExp is carried, not analysed. No ATAC analysis. There is no peak calling (Signac-style CallPeaks), no ArchR/SnapATAC-style tile matrix construction, no TF footprinting, and no accessibility-based annotation. The ATAC altExp is carried, not analysed. No multiome preprocessing. There is no cell-level linking step for 10x Multiome output; that happens upstream in Cell Ranger ARC, and sclet assumes you arrive with an object whose RNA and ATAC agree on cells. No modality-specific workflow. RunMultimodalWorkflow() registers modalities and stops. It does not dispatch to any analysis, which is why the record’s method is "multimodal_mainline" and its summary contains only has_ADT / has_ATAC. No evidence from the AI layer. The three multimodal actions are all read-only and all write nothing. There is no multimodal evidence node kind, so no AI answer can cite a multimodal result — because there is no multimodal result to cite. The reason for the gap is not effort, it is the contract. Every other sclet mainline is built on the same three-layer pattern: a Run*() that computes, a typed state record that stores what was computed, and a plot_* / get_* pair that reads it back. A modality backend has to be honest about which cells are comparable across modalities before it can write a record at all, and that question — matching, filtering, and what to do about cells present in one modality but not the other — is unsolved in the object contract. Registering the modality now, without computing on it, is what keeps the door open: when a backend arrives, altExp("ADT") and its multimodal_adt record are already the agreed entry point. 17.6 What to Do Today Until a backend exists, the honest route through multimodal data is: Attach the modality upstream with altExp(sce, "ADT") <- adt_sce and make sure the cells line up. sclet will not do this for you, and it will not silently subset. Register it with register_multimodal_adt() (or RunMultimodalWorkflow() for both modalities) so the object’s state layer records that the modality exists and how large it is. Analyse the modality in your own code — the barcode-level ADT or ATAC work is a script, not a Run*() call. Keep the RNA analysis on the mainlines. Clustering, annotation, trajectory and differential analysis all read the RNA assay; a multimodal object is still a valid input to every chapter before this one. Use check_multimodal_readiness() as the answer to “what does sclet think this object has?” — it distinguishes attached from registered and never implies an analysis has been run. # The end state of the recommended route, on the demo object: attached and # registered, with nothing computed. registered <- summarize_multimodal_evidence(demo_multimodal) c(modalities = registered$n_modalities, kinds = paste(registered$modality_kinds, collapse = ","), raw_values = registered$raw_values_included) ## modalities kinds raw_values ## "1" "ADT" "FALSE" # A real CITE-seq object: the ADT counts come from your own Cell Ranger run. # Why not executed here: the book has no CITE-seq dataset, and attaching a # fabricated ADT matrix would document a result that cannot be reproduced. adt_sce <- Read10X("path/to/adt/filtered_feature_bc_matrix/") common <- intersect(colnames(sce), colnames(adt_sce)) sce <- sce[, common] altExp(sce, "ADT") <- adt_sce[, common] sce <- register_multimodal_adt(sce, name = "cite_ADT") check_multimodal_readiness(sce) summarize_multimodal_evidence(sce)

18 Enhanced Visualization Once a dataset has been processed, plotting becomes the main way we inspect whether the workflow is behaving as expected. We need to check clusters, marker expression, sample composition, and structured summaries across groups, often with many small figure adjustments along the way. sclet provides an enhanced visualization ecosystem tightly integrated with the ggsc package. It offers high-level plotting functions that operate directly on SingleCellExperiment objects while still returning standard ggplot2 objects, so you keep both convenience and full downstream customizability. The chapter has two halves, and they are tested differently. The general-purpose plots (dimensional reduction, heatmaps, composition) run on the shared pbmc object during book rendering. The module-specific plots consume typed state records from analysis modules, so they are demonstrated on cached objects from earlier chapters or, where no suitable cache exists, shown as callable examples that state exactly which prerequisite is missing. Every non-executed chunk below says why in a comment on the chunk itself. 18.1 Loading data library(sclet) 18.2 Dimensionality Reduction Plots sclet wraps ggsc::sc_dim and ggsc::sc_feature to provide CellDimPlot and FeatureDimPlot. These functions automatically resolve the active reduction and layer from the object’s state. 18.2.1 CellDimPlot CellDimPlot is used to visualize categorical cell metadata on a reduced dimensional space (e.g., UMAP, PCA). library(ggplot2) library(aplot) # Visualize clustering results p1 <- CellDimPlot(pbmc, group.by = "ident") + ggtitle("Clusters") # Visualize batch or other metadata # Assuming we have a 'label' column in colData if ("label" %in% colnames(colData(pbmc))) { p2 <- CellDimPlot(pbmc, group.by = "label") + ggtitle("Cell Types") plot_list(p1, p2) } else { p1 } 18.2.2 FeatureDimPlot FeatureDimPlot is used to visualize continuous variables, such as gene expression levels, on the reduced dimensional space. # Visualize expression of specific marker genes FeatureDimPlot(pbmc, features = c("MS4A1", "CD8A")) 18.3 Expression Heatmaps GroupHeatmap provides a convenient way to visualize the average expression of features across different cell groups using scater::plotGroupedHeatmap. # Define a set of marker genes markers <- c("IL7R", "CD14", "LYZ", "MS4A1", "CD8A", "FCGR3A", "MS4A7") # Plot average expression by cluster GroupHeatmap(pbmc, features = markers, group.by = "ident", scale = TRUE) 18.4 Cell Statistics CellStatPlot is useful for visualizing the composition of cell groups (e.g., cell type proportions across different conditions). # If we have multiple samples or batches, we can plot the proportion of each cluster # Here we just use a simulated 'batch' column for demonstration if one doesn't exist if (!"batch" %in% colnames(colData(pbmc))) { set.seed(123) pbmc$batch <- sample(c("Sample1", "Sample2"), ncol(pbmc), replace = TRUE) } # `CellStatPlot()` has no `stat.by` parameter: `group.by` is the x aesthetic and # `split.by` is what fills/blocks it. Passing a non-existent argument used to be # forwarded to `geom_bar()` through `...` and surfaced as the warning # "Ignoring unknown parameters: `stat.by`" -- silent in a rendered book, but it # meant the plot was drawing something other than the documented composition # (measured 2026-10-21). CellStatPlot(pbmc, group.by = "ident", split.by = "batch", position = "fill") + ylab("Proportion") + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) These visualization functions are designed to minimize boilerplate code while remaining fully compatible with ggplot2 grammar (+ theme(), + scale_color_manual(), etc.). 18.5 Module-Specific Visualization Beyond the general-purpose plotting functions, sclet provides specialized visualization functions for each analysis module. These consume the typed state records directly, so you never need to manually extract matrices or metadata columns. Each module plot needs two things: the function, and an object carrying the matching record. The functions are all implemented and all return ggplot objects; what varies is whether the book has an object to hand. The sections below are split accordingly, and each chunk’s comment names the prerequisite. 18.5.1 Trajectory and Fate The trajectory and fate plots read the records written by RunTrajectoryWorkflow(), RunVelocity() and RunCellFate(). The book has cached objects for both halves, so the figures below are produced from real recorded results rather than described: the trajectory panels use the cached pancreas object through RunTrajectoryWorkflow(), the same object the cell fate chapter uses; the velocity and fate panels use data/hermann-sperm-dynamics.rds, which already carries a recorded cellrank analysis. library(aplot) # The workflow record must exist before any panel can be drawn. panc_viz <- readRDS("data/pancreas_sub_sce.rds") panc_viz <- RunTrajectoryWorkflow( panc_viz, group = "SubCellType", reduction = "UMAP", run_diffusion_map = TRUE, run_slingshot = TRUE, run_velocity = "never", run_fate = "never", name = "pancreas_viz" ) # One call assembles the panels that have records behind them. plot_trajectory_overview( panc_viz, id = "pancreas_viz", panels = c("lineage") ) fate_demo <- readRDS("data/hermann-sperm-dynamics.rds") # Fate probability on the embedding, for one lineage. plot_fate_probability(fate_demo, fate = 1, reduction = "UMAP", id = "cellrank") # Terminal state assignments. plot_fate_terminal_states(fate_demo, reduction = "UMAP", id = "cellrank") # Lineage driver trends: which genes trend along pseudotime / fate probability. cellrank_record <- get_cellrank(fate_demo, id = "cellrank") lineage <- cellrank_record$artifacts$fate_probability_names[[1]] plot_fate_driver_trends(fate_demo, lineage = lineage, top_n = 4, id = "cellrank") # Velocity latent time on the same embedding. plot_velocity_latent_time(fate_demo, reduction = "UMAP") 18.5.2 Program and Regulon Activity Gene set scores and regulons share a unified visualization layer. The source parameter lets you switch between "geneset_scoring" and "scenic" without changing the plot call. The plots need recorded program scores. None of the book’s cached objects carries a geneset_scoring record, so the chunk below scores the shared pbmc object first: RunGeneSetScoring() is pure R with a UCell backend, so this is a real run and the three figures are produced from real scores. # Score a few small signatures so the program plots have a record to read. program_signatures <- list( T_cell = c("CD3D", "CD3E", "CD8A", "CD4"), B_cell = c("CD79A", "MS4A1"), Myeloid = c("LYZ", "CD14", "FCGR3A") ) pbmc_program <- RunGeneSetScoring(pbmc, gene_sets = program_signatures, method = "UCell", name = "ucell_viz") # Single program on the embedding. plot_program_activity(pbmc_program, program = "T_cell", source = "geneset_scoring", id = "ucell_viz") # Multi-program heatmap across groups. plot_program_heatmap(pbmc_program, programs = names(program_signatures), source = "geneset_scoring", group.by = "colLabels", id = "ucell_viz") # Program dotplot: size = percent expressing, color = mean activity. plot_program_dotplot(pbmc_program, programs = names(program_signatures), source = "geneset_scoring", group.by = "colLabels", id = "ucell_viz") SCENIC regulon activity is a different source on the same functions. It is not executed here because the SCENIC record is not available in the book build — see the regulon section of the program chapter: # Why not executed: plot_scenic_activity() reads a SCENIC altExp written by # RunSCENIC(), which needs the pySCENIC basilisk environment plus a cisTarget # ranking database. The book build has the small reference files but not that # database, so no SCENIC record exists on any cached object. plot_scenic_activity(pbmc_program, regulon = "STAT1(+)", source = "scenic") 18.5.3 Perturbation Priority # `plot_perturbation_ranking()` reads the Augur record written by # `RunPerturbationPriority()`. On the shared `pbmc` object that record arrives # from the [State Priority](#state-priority) chapter, which runs earlier in the # book; the guard makes the dependency explicit instead of relying on chapter # order, and skips the chunk rather than erroring when the record is absent # (for example when Augur is not installed and that chapter's own chunks are # conditional too). plot_perturbation_ranking(pbmc, n = 15) 18.5.4 Spatial Analysis The spatial deconvolution plots read the cell-type proportion columns recorded by RunSpatialDeconvolution(). The cached Visium DLPFC object in the book carries the tissue and the colocalization/niche records, but it was built to demonstrate SVP, not deconvolution, so it has no c2l_* columns. Cell2location itself needs a paired reference and a Python environment, which the book build does not provision. The chunk below therefore attaches a deconvolution-shaped record to the cached object and draws both figures from it. Read carefully what that demonstrates: it exercises the plotting contract — record in, ranked bars and heatmap out — and it does not demonstrate deconvolution. The proportions are drawn at random, and the cell-type labels are labels, not estimates. spe <- readRDS("data/visium-dlpfc-sub.rds") # A deconvolution-shaped record, so the plotting contract can be exercised. # The proportions below are random: this is a plotting demo, not an estimate. set.seed(1) spatial_demo_cells <- c("L2.IT", "L4.IT", "L5.IT", "L6.IT") for (cell_type in spatial_demo_cells) { spe[[paste0("c2l_", cell_type)]] <- runif(ncol(spe), 0, 0.5) } spe <- sclet:::sclet_set_analysis(spe, "spatial_deconv", list( id = "viz_demo", method = "cell2location", artifacts = list(columns = paste0("c2l_", spatial_demo_cells)), timestamp = Sys.time() )) # Mean estimated proportion per cell type, ranked. plot_spatial_deconvolution(spe, n = 10) # Cell type x spot proportion heatmap. plot_spatial_composition(spe, n = 4) # Why not executed: cell2location needs a paired spatial object and scRNA-seq # reference with a shared gene space, plus a basilisk Python environment. The # comment above is not a substitute for this route, which produces real # proportions. sce_spatial <- RunSpatialDeconvolution( sce_spatial, sce_ref, ref_group_key = "cell_type", name = "my_deconv" ) plot_spatial_deconvolution(sce_spatial) 18.5.5 Cell-Cell Communication The communication plots read the standardized interaction table recorded by RunCCI(). The cached pancreas object plus a CellChat run is enough, so the three figures below are produced from real inferred interactions — the same run the communication chapter uses. # Real interactions for the plotting layer to read. cci_viz <- readRDS("data/pancreas_sub_sce.rds") cci_viz <- RunCCI(cci_viz, method = "CellChat", group = "CellType", layer = "logcounts", name = "cellchat_viz", species = "mouse", keep_object = TRUE) ## [1] "Create a CellChat object from a data matrix" ## Set cell identities for the new CellChat object ## The cell groups used for CellChat analysis are Ductal, Ngn3 low EP, Ngn3 high EP, Pre-endocrine, Endocrine ## The number of highly variable ligand-receptor pairs used for signaling inference is 342 ## triMean is used for calculating the average gene expression per cell group. ## [1] ">>> Run CellChat on sc/snRNA-seq data <<< [2026-10-22 14:19:12.673329]" ## [1] ">>> CellChat inference is done. Parameter values are stored in `object@options$parameter` <<< [2026-10-22 14:19:24.34776]" nrow(get_cci(cci_viz, id = "cellchat_viz")) ## [1] 65 # Bubble plot: one dot per interaction, size and colour by probability. plot_cci_bubble(cci_viz, id = "cellchat_viz") # Network view of the strongest signalling. plot_cci_network(cci_viz, id = "cellchat_viz") plot_cci_sigmoid(cci_viz, id = "cellchat_viz", top_n = 15) 18.5.6 Reference Mapping

20 Cell Identity and Reference Mapping chapter. Label transfer from a reference is cheap enough to demonstrate: a KNN mapping of pbmc against a held-out subset of itself gives a mapping record with a real transferred-label column and a real score column, which is exactly what the two functions read. The KNN path is deliberate. SingleR/celldex mapping is already demonstrated in the reference mapping chapter, but it downloads a reference atlas and is conditional on those packages; for a visualization example the requirement is a record, not a specific backend. set.seed(11) ref_index <- sample(seq_len(ncol(pbmc)), 500) ref_sce <- pbmc[, ref_index] query_sce <- pbmc[, -ref_index] ref_sce$label <- as.character(SingleCellExperiment::colLabels(ref_sce)) query_sce <- RunReferenceMapping( object = query_sce, ref = ref_sce, labels = "label", method = "KNN", layer = "logcounts", k = 5, name = "knn_viz" ) # Both columns the two plots resolve from the mapping record. get_mapping(query_sce, id = "knn_viz")$artifacts[c("labels_col", "score_col")] ## $labels_col ## [1] "knn_viz_labels" ## ## $score_col ## [1] "knn_viz_score" # Label transfer summary heatmap: query groups x transferred labels. plot_reference_label_transfer_heatmap(query_sce, group.by = "colLabels", id = "knn_viz") # Per-label confidence distribution. plot_reference_label_confidence(query_sce, id = "knn_viz")

21 Metacells with SuperCell 21.1 RunSuperCell 21.2 Estimate SuperCell Purity

21 Metacells with SuperCell As single-cell datasets continue to grow, it is often useful to replace highly redundant individual cells with a smaller number of representative metacells. This reduces computational burden, improves robustness in some downstream analyses, and can make large datasets easier to interpret. In sclet, this workflow is exposed through RunSuperCell(), which wraps the SuperCell package while keeping the result inside a SingleCellExperiment-compatible workflow. In this chapter, we use the pbmc4k dataset introduced earlier in the batch-correction chapter. Because SuperCell is installed in the bookdown GitHub Actions workflow, the examples in this chapter are executed during documentation build and therefore also serve as regression checks. 21.1 RunSuperCell The RunSuperCell() function provides the main entry point for metacell construction. sce_sc <- RunSuperCell(pbmc4k, gamma = 5) sce_sc ## class: SingleCellExperiment ## dim: 33694 746 ## metadata(1): sclet ## assays(2): counts logcounts ## rownames(33694): RP11-34P13.3 FAM138A ... AC213203.1 ## FAM231B ## rowData names(9): ENSEMBL_ID Symbol_TENx ... p.value ## FDR ## colnames: NULL ## colData names(1): size ## reducedDimNames(0): ## mainExpName: NULL ## altExpNames(0): The output of RunSuperCell() is a SingleCellExperiment object whose columns now represent metacells rather than individual cells. From this point on, you can continue with a fairly standard downstream workflow. post_process <- function(sce) { sce <- NormalizeData(sce) sce <- FindVariableFeatures(sce) sce <- ScaleData(sce) sce <- RunPCA(sce, subset_row = VariableFeatures(sce), layer = "scaled") sce <- FindNeighbors(sce, dims = 1:10) sce <- FindClusters(sce) sce <- RunUMAP(sce) return(sce) } sce_sc <- post_process(sce_sc) library(ggsc) sc_dim(sce_sc, reduction="UMAP") + sc_dim_geom_label() 21.2 Estimate SuperCell Purity pbmc4k2 <- post_process(pbmc4k) SC <- get_supercell(sce_sc, element = "object") purity <- SuperCell::supercell_purity(colLabels(pbmc4k2), SC$membership, method = "entropy") head(purity) ## 1 2 3 4 5 6 ## 0 0 0 0 0 0 summary(purity) ## Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. ## 0.00000 0.00000 0.00000 0.02202 0.00000 0.95027

23 Phenotype Association 23.1 A practical pattern 23.2 What gets recorded

23 Phenotype Association Single-cell data often becomes most interesting when it can be connected back to cohort-level outcomes: survival, response, progression, or any other phenotype that is measured in bulk but not directly annotated for each cell. This is exactly the bridge that RunPhenotypeAssociation() is meant to provide. The current sclet implementation wraps scPAS, transfers the result back to the SingleCellExperiment object, and records the provenance in the analysis-state. In practice, this makes the single-cell object the place where cell-level association scores, model parameters, and downstream visualization all meet again. 23.1 A practical pattern The important thing is not the toy syntax, but the data alignment: the single-cell object and the bulk matrix must share a comparable gene universe, the phenotype vector or table must match the bulk samples, and the phenotype family (gaussian, binomial, cox) must reflect the actual study design. To keep the example grounded, the template below uses package-backed real data instead of a fabricated pseudo-bulk matrix: TENxPBMCData provides the single-cell object and airway provides a bulk RNA-seq cohort with a real treatment phenotype. The biology is still only a mechanics demo rather than a matched study design, but at least the data source is a proper R package instead of something we invented on the spot. # Not executed: needs the `scPAS` package, which is not on CRAN or # Bioconductor, plus a bulk cohort whose phenotypes match the single-cell # object. `airway` is a real cohort but it is not a PBMC cohort, so the # template shows the mechanics and is not a runnable study design. library(TENxPBMCData) library(airway) # Use a package-backed single-cell dataset. # We intentionally keep Ensembl-style rownames here because the airway bulk # dataset also uses Ensembl identifiers. sce_pheno <- TENxPBMCData::TENxPBMCData("pbmc3k") sce_pheno <- sce_pheno[, seq_len(min(500, ncol(sce_pheno)))] # Use a package-backed bulk cohort with a real binary phenotype. data("airway", package = "airway") bulk_matrix <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(airway) phenotype_data <- as.character(SummarizedExperiment::colData(airway)$dex) # Align the gene universe explicitly before fitting. common_genes <- intersect(rownames(sce_pheno), rownames(bulk_matrix)) sce_pheno <- sce_pheno[common_genes, ] bulk_matrix <- bulk_matrix[common_genes, , drop = FALSE] sce_pheno <- RunPhenotypeAssociation( sce_pheno, bulk_matrix = bulk_matrix, phenotype_data = phenotype_data, family = "binomial" ) head(as.data.frame(SummarizedExperiment::colData(sce_pheno))) S4Vectors::metadata(sce_pheno)$phenotype_assoc 23.2 What gets recorded Once the model runs successfully, RunPhenotypeAssociation() writes the cell-level outputs back into colData(sce) and stores the recovered scPAS model metadata in metadata(sce)$phenotype_assoc. This means the result behaves like any other tracked module in sclet: you can inspect what happened, keep it with the object, and pass it downstream without inventing a second sidecar file format.

24 Interactive Data Exploration 24.1 Launch Explorer 24.2 Customization

24 Interactive Data Exploration Not every question is easiest to answer from a static figure or a scripted summary. Sometimes the fastest way to understand a dataset is to click, filter, inspect, and compare interactively. sclet integrates iSEE to provide a Shiny-based interactive explorer for your SingleCellExperiment objects. The examples in this chapter are shown but not executed during book rendering, because they launch an interactive Shiny session rather than producing a static result that can be embedded cleanly in the book. In other words, the issue here is not package availability but session lifetime: a documentation build should finish, whereas an interactive explorer is expected to stay open until the user closes it. 24.1 Launch Explorer You can launch the explorer directly from your R console: To reproduce this locally, the only real prerequisites are an SCE object with at least one usable assay and dimensional reduction, plus the iSEE package. library(sclet) sce <- pbmc # Launch the app RunExplorer(sce) This will open a web browser where you can: Visualize reduced dimensions (UMAP, PCA) Explore gene expression on the plot Check column data (QC metrics, Clusters) Select points and inspect data 24.2 Customization RunExplorer passes additional arguments to iSEE::iSEE(), allowing you to pre-configure panels. # Example: Start with just a ReducedDimensionPlot and a FeaturePlot library(iSEE) initial <- list( ReducedDimensionPlot(PanelId=1L), FeatureAssayPlot(PanelId=1L) ) RunExplorer(sce, initial = initial)

In many settings, the real question is whether a predefined biological program, pathway, or cell-type signature is active in a given cell or spatial location. The SVP ecosystem is designed for this use case. This chapter shows how gene set activity can be quantified and explored in both single-cell and spatial settings, using SingleCellExperiment-compatible workflows. External agent driving. A general-purpose coding agent runs in the user’s own session, inspects the object through exported functions, plans a set of actions, and executes them through the package. This is the book’s mainline route: it needs no in-package model, keeps the conversation in the user’s own tooling, and is the route an experienced user can inspect step by step. In-package assistant. The package itself talks to a model through aisdk, plans, asks for clarification, and executes. It is the lower-friction route: less setup and less control, and it needs a configured model. Both routes end in the same place, which is the principle this part keeps returning to: the engine is the authority, not the model. A model may propose an analysis, but it does not perform one. Plans are validated against the live object, confirmation is carried by a token minted for that exact plan, execution walks the plan one action at a time, and results are recorded so that a report can be recomputed from the ledger rather than retold from the conversation. When a plan is illegal, the engine refuses it; when a step cannot run, the failure is recorded as a failure. The chapters therefore read in one direction: the one-call route first, then the concepts, then the driving route, then the in-package route, and finally the governance layer that keeps claims tied to the evidence actually recorded. If you have five minutes, read AI in One Call and stop. It is two commands and it is the whole user-facing surface for a first-time user.

26 AI in One Call This chapter is the shortest path from an installed package to an AI-assisted analysis. It is written for someone who has never used the AI layer and does not yet care how it works. Read it once, run the two commands, and come back for the rest of the part when you want to know what happened. Everything here is real: no chunk is \dontrun, and the ones that call a model are gated the same way as the rest of the book, so on a machine with no provider they are skipped rather than failed. 26.1 What you need first The AI layer is optional. One package, installed once: # Not executed: this is a machine-level action, not a chunk. install.packages("aisdk") scletAI() checks this before anything is sent, so a missing package is an error that names the command rather than a plan that reaches a provider and fails there. And one provider key in ~/.Renviron, which R reads at startup (restart afterwards): # Not executed: never print a key into a rendered book. # OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... sclet never asks for the key and never sees it: aisdk reads it from the environment and the model provider bills the call. A call is also non-deterministic — the same goal can produce a different plan — which is why the layer records what it did rather than trusting what it said. 26.2 The one call # `conflicted` refuses a `library()` while a name exists in several attached # packages. The book's setup chunk prefers base's `intersect`/`union`/`setdiff` # BEFORE the later chapters attach GenomicRanges (via SVP), and a preference # does not apply retroactively to a package attached after it was set -- so it # is set again here, where the AI path begins. Same choice, one line. for (fn in c("intersect", "union", "setdiff")) { try(conflicted::conflicts_prefer(fn, base::get(fn), .quiet = TRUE), silent = TRUE) } set.seed(42) sce <- scuttle::mockSCE(ncells = 200, ngenes = 80) sce <- SingleCellExperiment::SingleCellExperiment( assays = list(counts = SummarizedExperiment::assay(sce, "counts")), colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(SummarizedExperiment::colData(sce)) ) sce <- NormalizeData(sce) sce <- FindVariableFeatures(sce) sce <- ScaleData(sce) dim(sce) ## [1] 80 200 Now describe what you want. scletAI() is the whole API: analysis <- scletAI(sce, "cluster the cells and find markers for each cluster") analysis ## sclet beginner AI analysis [invalid_plan] ## Goal: cluster the cells and find markers for each cluster The plan is printed, then the session asks [y/N]. In a script, pass confirm = "yes" to run without prompting, or confirm = "no" to see the plan and stop. On a machine with no provider this chunk is skipped by the same switch as the rest of the AI material, and the chapter still renders. 26.2.1 What came back, and what it means analysis$status is the one field to read. Three outcomes, all of them normal: status what happened what to do completed every action ran and was recorded read analysis$object — the clusters are on it dry_run the plan was previewed, not executed (you said no, or the session is non-interactive) run again with confirm = "yes" invalid_plan the engine refused the plan read analysis$report$errors; each names what to fix The refusal case is not a bug and not a misconfiguration: a language model proposes a plan, the engine checks it against the live object, and a plan that does not survive is refused before anything runs. That is the design — the alternative is an analysis whose steps were never checked. It is also non-deterministic: the same goal on the same object can propose a different plan on a different day, so a refusal is a retry, not a verdict. analysis$status ## [1] "invalid_plan" When it completes, the updated SingleCellExperiment is in analysis$object — the clusters and marker table are on it, exactly as if you had called FindClusters() and RunDEtest() yourself: if (identical(analysis$status, "completed")) { length(unique(as.character(analysis$object$ident))) } else { "no clusters: the plan did not complete" } ## [1] "no clusters: the plan did not complete" 26.3 What just happened scletAI() is one call, but it is not one mechanism. Underneath, in order: A plan was composed. A language model was given the object’s recorded state — what analyses exist, what assays are active, what is blocked — and asked for steps. It was never given your expression matrix. The plan was validated against the live object. Every action had to be a real registry key, every parameter a real one for it, every dependency satisfiable. An illegal plan is refused here, before anything runs. You approved it. Confirmation is a token minted for that exact plan and object state; a plan edited afterwards is refused rather than silently run. It executed one action at a time, each result recorded as an evidence node. A report was rendered from the ledger and re-checked — which is why the numbers in it can be recomputed rather than retold. The rest of this part is those five steps in detail, plus the route where you write the plan yourself. 26.4 The three other calls you will meet scletAI() is the door; these are the rooms, in the order a user meets them. 26.4.1 Ask it something, without running anything AskAI(sce, "What has been analysed so far, and what should I check next?") ## sclet AI result [copilot] ## Only one recorded analysis exists in the ledger: `preprocess::normalize_logcounts` (status `completed`, method `scuttle::calculateCPM + log1p`, inputs `counts`, scale factor 10000, 200 cells × 80 features), recorded as a `state` record with no parents (root of the recorded chain). A `scaled` assay/layer exists and is the active view with `last_command = "ScaleData"`, but no `ScaleData` record appears in `analyses`, `state_records`, `workflows`, or the timeline (timeline `n_steps = 1`), so scaling is visible in the object but undocumented in the ledger. `features.hvg` is reported (n = 2000, method `scran`, rowData columns mean, total, tech, bio, p.value, FDR), which conflicts with the 80-gene matrix and should be treated as unverified. Not present: reductions (`reductions = []`), graphs, clustering/identity levels (`n_levels = 0`), marker/DE tests, and any `ev:` evidence nodes. Blocked gates: trajectory (`reduction_missing`), differential abundance (`design_role_missing`, needs `ConfirmAIDesignSemantics()`), velocity (`spliced_unspliced_missing`), spatial (no spatial record), multimodal (no altExp). Design semantics are unconfirmed; `Treatment` is only a candidate condition column. The ambient-RNA screen label `low` (low-UMI tail share 0.0718, top-gene detection uniformity 0.7271) is a screen, not a measurement — no contamination estimate exists absent a `run_decontx` evidence node. `execute_analysis` capability is unknown and `available_actions` is empty. No causal or biological claims are supported. Recommended order: reconcile record vs object (scaled layer, HVG provenance), confirm design semantics, run descriptive QC spine on counts/logcounts, then run_pca → find_neighbors (→ optional clustering), then marker tests within clusters and condition contrasts only after design confirmation; optionally run_decontx if ambient contamination is suspected. ## Findings:10 Recommendations:6 Proposed actions:6 AskAI() is read-only: it answers from the recorded state and cannot change the object. It is the right call when you want to understand what you have before deciding what to do. 26.4.2 The same run with the switches visible RunAIAnalysis(sce, goal = "cluster the cells", confirm = "yes") ## sclet beginner AI analysis [completed] ## Goal: cluster the cells ## Actions: run_pca -> find_neighbors -> find_clusters ## Report self-check: passed RunAIAnalysis() is the engine scletAI() calls, with its arguments exposed: include to choose which action groups the planner may use, record to decide whether the round is written to the ledger, render_report and verify_before_continue for the self-check. Reach for it when the defaults are not what you want — not first. 26.4.3 Read a finished round back graph <- AnalysisGraph(analysis$object) graph ## <sclet trace graph> sclet-trace-graph/1 ## rounds: 0 ## nodes: 1 | edges: 0 AnalysisGraph() projects the round onto two tables: which step produced which record, and which step consumed which earlier step’s output. It is how you audit a run you did not write, and how an agent picks up where the last one stopped. 26.5 When it refuses Refusal is the layer working, not failing. The three you will meet first: what you see what it means sclet_ai_missing_dependency aisdk is not installed; the message names the command sclet_ai_missing_model no model could be resolved; supply one, or set a default plan_empty / action is not registered the model proposed nothing, or something that is not an action — the engine refused rather than guessing A provider error (a 401, a rate limit) is the provider’s, and arrives verbatim; sclet does not translate it. 26.6 What to read next Driving sclet from an External Agent — the route where you write the plan yourself, and the one most users end up on. AI Foundations — what an action declares, and what the registry exposes. Evidence Governance — why a report may only claim what the ledger supports. The short version: scletAI() to start, AskAI() to understand, RunAIAnalysis() when you need a switch, AnalysisGraph() to check.
