27 AI Foundations: State, Actions, and the Ledger Every other chapter in this book describes analysis you run yourself: you call RunDEtest(), you look at the plot, you decide. This chapter describes a different mode. You describe a goal, and something else runs the analysis — an AI agent inside the package, or an agent you talk to from outside R, or your own script written against a contract. All three modes run on the same three components, and all three are only as trustworthy as those components. This chapter explains them, because a plan you cannot read is a plan you cannot audit. 27.1 The problem: a script is a decision you cannot re-examine The usual script is a straight line: # Not executed: `sce` is a placeholder and the point is the SHAPE of the script # -- four calls with no record of why. The same four calls run for real in the # [core workflow](#core-workflow) chapter, with the state they leave behind. sce <- NormalizeData(sce) sce <- FindVariableFeatures(sce) sce <- FindClusters(sce) sce <- RunDEtest(sce) Shown, not executed: this is the shape of the problem, not a runnable example. sce is a placeholder, and the same four calls appear as real, executing code in the core workflow. That is fine while you are the one running it. But notice what it does not record: why these thresholds, whether step 3 was even correct for this object, and what any of it implies. If a reviewer asks “how do you know your clusters were not an artifact of the batch effect?”, the script cannot answer, because the script never knew. sclet’s AI layer is built on the opposite premise. The object already carries its own history — the state contract from state-aware analysis. The AI layer’s job is to make that history something that can be planned against, validated, and audited instead of merely read. 27.2 The AIAction contract An action is the unit of AI work in sclet. It is not a function you call directly; it is a descriptor that declares what would happen if you did, tightly enough that the engine can refuse a plan that will not work. AIAction() takes: argument what it declares name the stable key a plan must match exactly handler the function that runs, receiving (object, params) description one line, shown to a planner prerequisites a function returning TRUE, FALSE, or a string explaining why not input_schema per-parameter types, or enumerations returns "sce" (returns the object) or "value" requires_confirmation whether a human must approve before execution output_schema what a later step may reference mutates_object, allowed_state_types what state the handler may write estimated_cost, idempotent cost label, and whether repeating is safe planner_visible whether a model may propose it, or only a person writing the plan replaces_object whether the handler returns a different object (an aggregation, say) Four of those do the real work: prerequisites returns a reason, not just a boolean. An action whose object has no batch column is not “unavailable”; it says the parameter is missing, which the caller can act on. This is what lets a planner propose a fix instead of guessing why it failed. allowed_state_types bounds what a handler may write. An action that only reads cannot add a reduction; an integration action cannot quietly rewrite the clustering. A plan that violates this is refused by the engine, not merely deprecated in a style guide. estimated_cost is honest. Most of the registry is cheap; the expensive end is a Python model fit that runs for minutes to hours — SCENIC’s regulon inference, CellOracle’s in-silico perturbation, RegVelo, cell2location deconvolution. Those also ask for explicit confirmation before they start, because a multi-hour run is a decision, not a default. planner_visible separates “registered” from “plannable”. Some analyses need an input only the user has: a gene set, a bulk phenotype matrix, a reference SingleCellExperiment, a GRN prior, a pySCENIC database. An action over such an input is still registered, still validated, still executed — but a model cannot invent the input it requires, so the action is marked planner_visible = FALSE and left out of the catalog a planner is shown. It remains available to you, writing the plan by hand, which is the subject of the next chapter. 27.3 The registry only exposes what this object can actually run AIDefaultExecutionRegistry() returns the actions available on the object you hand it. Prerequisites are evaluated, not advertised: an action the object cannot satisfy is listed together with the reason, so a refusal is something you can read and act on. One distinction matters from here on. The registry is the executable catalog; the catalog a model is shown is a subset of it, minus the actions marked planner_visible = FALSE. So include = "all" means “every action this package offers”, not “every action a model may propose” — the difference is the handful whose input only you can supply. library(sclet) sce <- SingleCellExperiment::SingleCellExperiment( list(counts = matrix(1, nrow = 10, ncol = 8)) ) reg <- AIDefaultExecutionRegistry(sce, include = "read") length(reg) ## [1] 3 names(reg) ## [1] "inspect_status" "inspect_ledger" "check_qc" # The full executable catalog, and how much of it a model may propose. all_actions <- AIDefaultExecutionRegistry(sce, include = "all") length(all_actions) ## [1] 46 sum(vapply(all_actions, function(a) isTRUE(a$planner_visible), logical(1L))) ## [1] 37 The include argument selects groups. "read" is the deliberately small default — the inspection group, none of which modify the object. Requesting "all" exposes the analysis groups, each carrying the same confirmation requirements it had before you asked for it, and every one of them appears in the second count unless planner_visible says otherwise. The numbers are worth reading as a pair: the executable catalog is larger than the planner’s, and the gap is exactly the actions whose input you must supply yourself. 27.4 The ledger is the only authority GetAnalysisLedger() projects the object’s state into a bounded, model-facing summary: the active view, recorded analyses, lineage, the actions available right now, the fingerprint, and — crucially — analysis_story, the plain-language account of what this object has been through. ledger <- GetAnalysisLedger(sce) names(ledger) ## [1] "schema_version" "sclet_version" ## [3] "sclet_installed_at" "dataset" ## [5] "active_view" "active_states" ## [7] "features" "health" ## [9] "analyses" "state_records" ## [11] "workflows" "lineage" ## [13] "analysis_story" "capabilities" ## [15] "blocked_actions" "quality_checks" ## [17] "available_actions" "warnings" ## [19] "fingerprint" ledger$fingerprint ## [1] "sclet-ai-747aba50" Nothing about the AI layer is stored separately. Evidence, claims, and results are state records like any other, so they survive saveRDS(), are visible in Status(), and cannot drift out of sync with the object they describe. That property is what makes the next two chapters possible: a plan is validated against the ledger, and a result is only ever as strong as the evidence the ledger can show for it.

28 Driving sclet from an External Agent This is the mainline of the AI layer, and the one most users will actually run. The package can plan an analysis itself if you configure a model provider, and the next chapter covers that. But that path has a cost and a dependency: it needs aisdk, a key, and a networked call for every plan. This chapter needs none of them. You are the planner. You read the shipped skills, write the plan as an R list, and let sclet validate and execute it under exactly the guardrails a built-in model would face. The division of labour is worth stating precisely, because it is the whole design: who decides you, the planner what should be analysed, in what order, with which parameters sclet whether that plan is even legal on this object, and what may be claimed afterwards A plan that survives validation is one the engine agreed to execute. That is not the same as good — the skills in inst/skills/ carry the domain knowledge that separates a legal plan from a useful one. 28.1 Read the skills first sclet ships four skills — plain SKILL.md files under inst/skills/, readable by any agent and by you. library(sclet) skills <- AISkills() skills ## [1] "sclet-analysis" "sclet-claims" "sclet-driver" ## [4] "sclet-provenance" guidelines <- ReadAISkill("sclet-analysis") nchar(guidelines$description) ## [1] 972 The analysis skill is the one to read before every plan: it encodes stage order, which steps produce evidence other steps need, and which parameters are modelling choices an agent must never make for the user. 28.2 A complete run The object below is deliberately small so this chapter executes during the book build. Everything here runs offline; no model is contacted at any point. library(sclet) set.seed(42) sce <- scuttle::mockSCE(ncells = 200, ngenes = 80) sce <- SingleCellExperiment::SingleCellExperiment( assays = list(counts = SummarizedExperiment::assay(sce, "counts")) ) dim(sce) ## [1] 80 200 28.2.1 1. What can run on this object? reg <- AIDefaultExecutionRegistry(sce, include = "all") length(reg) ## [1] 34 head(names(reg), 8) ## [1] "inspect_status" "inspect_ledger" ## [3] "check_qc" "normalize_data" ## [5] "find_variable_features" "scale_data" ## [7] "run_decontx" "run_pca" Ask for "all" deliberately here — a real plan needs the analysis groups, not just the read group. The registry is object-aware: an action whose prerequisites this object cannot meet is listed together with the reason. 28.2.2 2. Read the ledger, and bind the plan to it ledger <- GetAnalysisLedger(sce) ledger$fingerprint ## [1] "sclet-ai-746baa4a" The fingerprint is not decoration. Validation binds the plan to the state it was written against, so an object edited in between cannot accept a plan written for the old one. That is what makes the stateless pattern in the next section safe. 28.2.3 3. Write the plan plan <- new_sclet_ai_plan( task = "pbmc_markers", context_fingerprint = ledger$fingerprint, actions = list( list(id = "s1", action = "normalize_data"), list(id = "s2", action = "find_variable_features", params = list(nfeatures = 40L), depends_on = "s1"), list(id = "s3", action = "scale_data", depends_on = "s2"), list(id = "s4", action = "run_pca", params = list(ncomponents = 10L), depends_on = "s3"), list(id = "s5", action = "find_neighbors", params = list(dims = 1:10), depends_on = "s4"), list(id = "s6", action = "find_clusters", params = list(resolution = 1.0), depends_on = "s5"), list(id = "s7", action = "run_de_test", params = list(name = "markers"), depends_on = "s6") ) ) Three rules the engine enforces, so plan to them: every action is a verbatim registry key — a plausible-looking name is refused every params value matches the declared type in input_schema every ${step_id.output.field} reference has a matching depends_on 28.2.4 4. Validate — and read the errors validation <- ValidateAIPlan(plan, object = sce, registry = reg) validation$valid ## [1] TRUE validation$requires_confirmation ## [1] TRUE ValidateAIPlan() returns the errors, and unlike an exception they are the useful kind: it names the received value, and for a malformed reference it names the corrected spelling. A refusal at this point is progress — it costs nothing. 28.2.5 5. Dry-run, then execute ExecuteAIPlan() defaults to dry_run = TRUE, which returns what would run and changes nothing. Non-dry execution requires the confirmation token from this validation object: dry <- ExecuteAIPlan(sce, plan, registry = reg, validation = validation) dry$status ## [1] "dry_run" vapply(dry$results, function(r) r$status, character(1)) ## [1] "planned" "planned" "planned" "planned" "planned" ## [6] "planned" "planned" executed <- ExecuteAIPlan(sce, plan, registry = reg, validation = validation, dry_run = FALSE, confirmation = validation$confirmation_token) executed$status ## [1] "completed" vapply(executed$results, function(r) r$status, character(1)) ## [1] "completed" "completed" "completed" "completed" ## [5] "completed" "completed" "completed" Passing only confirmation without validation makes the engine re-validate and mint a token that can never match. Take both from one fresh validation. 28.2.6 6. This is the audit trail, and it is what the last chapter of this part is about. 28.3 Advancing in rounds ExecuteAIPlan() walks the plan in order with per-step retry. Nothing in execution rewrites later steps. A multi-stage analysis is therefore a sequence of plans, and starting each one is your decision. The reason is measured, not stylistic: recording a round changes the object’s fingerprint, so the previous plan is refused afterwards by design. again <- ValidateAIPlan(plan, object = executed$object, registry = reg) again$valid ## [1] FALSE again$errors ## [1] "plan context fingerprint does not match the current object" An old plan not being reusable is the feature: the plan you checked described a different object than the one you now hold. Two rules follow from the round boundary: A plan may only reference steps of its own plan. ${old_step.output.detest_id} across a round is refused. Carry a value forward by naming the record that produced it — detest_id = "markers" — which the ledger in front of you supplies literally. Re-validate every time. The fingerprint binds the plan to the object state it was validated against. Start a new round when a stage finished and the next feeds on it, when a step failed for a reason that changes the route, when the plan never covered the goal (plan$metadata$goal_coverage$missing), or when the user answered an open choice. 28.4 What you can do that a model cannot The registry has two audiences. A model is shown the actions it can actually fill; a few analyses need an input that exists only on your side — a gene set, a bulk phenotype matrix, a reference SingleCellExperiment, a GRN prior, a pySCENIC database. Those actions are registered and executable, but they are marked planner_visible = FALSE and kept out of a model’s catalog, because a plan proposing one of them would fail on a parameter no model can produce. Writing the plan yourself, you can use them. include = "all" means “every action this package offers”, and the difference from what a planner sees is exactly this list. all_actions <- AIDefaultExecutionRegistry(sce, include = "all") driver_only <- names(all_actions)[ !vapply(all_actions, function(a) isTRUE(a$planner_visible), logical(1L)) ] driver_only ## [1] "map_reference_knn" ## [2] "map_reference_symphony" ## [3] "run_regvelo" ## [4] "run_geneset_scoring" ## [5] "run_supercell" ## [6] "run_phenotype_association" ## [7] "run_scenic" ## [8] "run_in_silico_perturbation" ## [9] "run_spatial_deconvolution" Each one names, in its input_schema, what you have to bring. That is not a courtesy: ValidateAIPlan() refuses the step without it, and the refusal names the parameter rather than the action. 28.5 The plan you ran is a graph, and it outlives the session A round is not a list of steps in a log file. Each step that writes an analysis record is attributed to the record it produced, and steps that feed other steps keep the edge the plan declared. AnalysisGraph() projects that onto two tables you can read, print, or hand to another agent. graph <- AnalysisGraph(executed$object) graph ## <sclet trace graph> sclet-trace-graph/1 ## rounds: 1 (1 without stored topology) ## nodes: 14 | edges: 10 head(graph$edges, 8) ## from ## 1 step:ai_execution_plan_pbmc_markers_20261022144927_1jf4n6n3_20261022144930:s1 ## 2 step:ai_execution_plan_pbmc_markers_20261022144927_1jf4n6n3_20261022144930:s2 ## 3 step:ai_execution_plan_pbmc_markers_20261022144927_1jf4n6n3_20261022144930:s3 ## 4 step:ai_execution_plan_pbmc_markers_20261022144927_1jf4n6n3_20261022144930:s4 ## 5 step:ai_execution_plan_pbmc_markers_20261022144927_1jf4n6n3_20261022144930:s5 ## 6 step:ai_execution_plan_pbmc_markers_20261022144927_1jf4n6n3_20261022144930:s6 ## 7 step:ai_execution_plan_pbmc_markers_20261022144927_1jf4n6n3_20261022144930:s7 ## 8 record:clustering::louvain_clusters ## to ## 1 round:ai_execution_plan_pbmc_markers_20261022144927_1jf4n6n3_20261022144930 ## 2 round:ai_execution_plan_pbmc_markers_20261022144927_1jf4n6n3_20261022144930 ## 3 round:ai_execution_plan_pbmc_markers_20261022144927_1jf4n6n3_20261022144930 ## 4 round:ai_execution_plan_pbmc_markers_20261022144927_1jf4n6n3_20261022144930 ## 5 round:ai_execution_plan_pbmc_markers_20261022144927_1jf4n6n3_20261022144930 ## 6 round:ai_execution_plan_pbmc_markers_20261022144927_1jf4n6n3_20261022144930 ## 7 round:ai_execution_plan_pbmc_markers_20261022144927_1jf4n6n3_20261022144930 ## 8 record:graph::knn_graph ## kind parent_kind declared_input ## 1 step_of <NA> <NA> ## 2 step_of <NA> <NA> ## 3 step_of <NA> <NA> ## 4 step_of <NA> <NA> ## 5 step_of <NA> <NA> ## 6 step_of <NA> <NA> ## 7 step_of <NA> <NA> ## 8 consumed <NA> graph nrow(graph$nodes[graph$nodes$kind == "step", ]) ## [1] 7 Two questions this answers that a printed log cannot: which step produced a named record, and which later steps declared a given step as upstream. # Which step produced the marker table this round registered? marker_record <- graph$edges$to[graph$edges$kind == "produced" & grepl("detest", graph$edges$to)] graph_producers(graph, marker_record[1]) ## $ids ## character(0) ## ## $complete ## [1] FALSE # Which later steps declared the round's first step as upstream? first_step <- graph$nodes$id[graph$nodes$kind == "step"][1] graph_consumers(graph, first_step) ## $ids ## character(0) ## ## $complete ## [1] FALSE Both queries return the answer and whether the round that produced it carries a full trace. A record with no producer edge is not an error to chase: it may simply predate the trace, or have been written outside a plan. The graph is a projection over the object’s own records, so it survives saveRDS() with them, and a round that ran before this book existed is still readable — it simply reports complete = FALSE for that round, because the topology was never stored for it. Two things it will not show, and both are recorded rather than hidden. A re-run that re-writes an existing record id appears as a refreshed edge from the newer step, not as a second copy of the record, because the record store overwrites by id. And an action that returns a different object — metacell aggregation is the one — takes the earlier records with it; the graph says so with meta$object_replaced instead of silently dropping the rounds. 28.6 Resuming across processes The ledger lives on the object, so the whole analysis survives saveRDS(). An agent does not need a resident R session: each interaction can be a fresh Rscript that reads the object, plans the next stage against the fingerprint it carries, executes, and saves it back. Because is.character(validation$plan_id) — the id in the validation object — must match, and the fingerprint must still be current, a stale plan is refused rather than silently run. 28.7 Things not to attempt An empty plan is not a plan. Zero actions are refused (plan_empty) instead of reporting status = "completed" with no results. If the goal needs no computation, answer directly. A plan has no conditional steps. “If this succeeds, also do X” is a second round, not a longer plan. Never claim without evidence. The report’s claims are capped by the evidence that supports them, which is the subject of evidence governance. RunAIPlan() is a convenience, not a different contract. It validates internally, so use it for the common case and ValidateAIPlan()/ExecuteAIPlan() separately when you need to inspect the validation object — for instance to present a refusal to a user before fixing it.

29 The In-Package Assistant The external-agent path has the package acting as an engine and you as the planner. This chapter covers the other arrangement: the package also writes the plan, by asking a language model what to do. That convenience is real, and so is its price. sclet needs aisdk, a configured provider, and a network call for every plan. The chunks here are therefore gated on SCLET_BOOKDOWN_EVAL_AI rather than on the package alone: on a machine with a provider configured they execute and the outputs below are real, and on a machine without one — a CI runner, most of them — they are skipped. Rendered prose that depends on a model’s mood is not a regression test, and a build that quietly spends credits is not a build. 29.1 Requirements library(sclet) # A default model, configured once through aisdk: aisdk::get_model() ## [1] "deepseek:deepseek-chat" # Everything else works without any further setup. `NULL` here means the # default, which is to inject the shipped skills; `getOption()` is used rather # than `options()` because the latter evaluates an unset name and errors. getOption("sclet.ai.use_skills") ## NULL options(sclet.ai.use_skills) controls whether the shipped skills are injected into the planning prompt. It is on by default, and the AI foundations chapter explains why the skills — not the inline prompt — carry knowledge-type rules such as stage ordering. 29.2 An object to ask about The examples below need an object with clusters to find markers in, and — for the audit section — an integration that exposes a corrected expression layer. Building both here keeps the chapter self-contained: set.seed(42) demo <- scuttle::mockSCE(ncells = 200, ngenes = 60) demo <- SingleCellExperiment::SingleCellExperiment( assays = list(counts = SummarizedExperiment::assay(demo, "counts")), colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(SummarizedExperiment::colData(demo)) ) demo$batch <- rep(c("donor_1", "donor_2"), each = 100) demo <- NormalizeData(demo) demo <- FindVariableFeatures(demo) demo <- ScaleData(demo) demo <- RunPCA(demo, ncomponents = 10) demo <- FindNeighbors(demo, dims = 1:10) demo <- FindClusters(demo, resolution = 1.0) demo$ident <- as.character(SingleCellExperiment::colLabels(demo)) length(unique(demo$ident)) ## [1] 5 29.3 AIPlanAnalysis: ask for a plan plan <- AIPlanAnalysis(demo, goal = "find markers that distinguish the clusters") plan$actions ## [[1]] ## [[1]]$id ## [1] "step_1" ## ## [[1]]$action ## [1] "run_de_test" ## ## [[1]]$params ## [[1]]$params$name ## [1] "cluster_markers" ## ## [[1]]$params$min.pct ## [1] 0.1 ## ## [[1]]$params$logfc.threshold ## [1] 0.25 ## ## ## [[1]]$depends_on ## character(0) ## ## [[1]]$description ## [1] "All-cluster marker path (no ident.1/ident.2/group) yields a marker table per cluster in one round; prerequisites logcounts and colLabels are both present." ## ## [[1]]$expected_outputs ## list() ## ## [[1]]$requires_confirmation ## [1] TRUE ## ## [[1]]$max_retries ## [1] 0 ## ## [[1]]$continue_on_error ## [1] FALSE You will see a warning on the way, and it is the privacy layer doing its job rather than a problem: sclet AI outbound payload requires user consent before use. Fields requiring consent were redacted: active_states.clustering, features.hvg.selected Those two fields are the clustering and the selected variable features. Both are results of the analysis, not inputs to it, so they are held back unless you say otherwise — the point of the ledger is that a model can plan the next step without being handed the answer. The plan above is still correct because it does not need them: “find markers that distinguish the clusters” is a goal, and the cluster labels are read locally at execution time. If a later round does need the feature set, pass privacy_consent = TRUE to the call that makes it, and know that you have chosen to share it. The result is an ordinary plan — the same structure you wrote by hand in the previous chapter — so it is validated, previewed and executed by exactly the same functions. AIPlanAnalysis() also spends one repair round against validation errors and goal coverage before returning, so what you get back has already been checked once. plan$metadata$goal_coverage$missing names goal items with no step behind them; a hand-written plan gets no such help, so check it yourself. 29.3.1 The registry has to match the goal AIPlanAnalysis() plans against every action group by default. RunAIAnalysis() differs: it defaults to a beginner registry — read, preprocess, dimred, graph, cluster — which is the right set for “run a pipeline from raw counts” and the wrong one for “find markers”, because run_de_test lives in the annotation group. What that costs you is worth watching once, because the failure is instructive rather than silent. With the beginner registry the planner is shown only its eleven actions, so for a marker goal it proposes a step it was never offered, and validation refuses the plan: action is not registered: run_de_test; it exists, but in the 'annotation' registry group, which this registry did not request -- add 'annotation' to include Two things are true at once here. The registry you pass is part of the question — pass the groups your goal needs. And the engine’s refusal tells you exactly how to fix it, because a bare “not registered” would have sent you looking for a typo. 29.4 RunAIAnalysis: plan, preview, ask, execute in one call result <- RunAIAnalysis(demo, goal = "find markers that distinguish the clusters", include = c("read", "preprocess", "dimred", "graph", "cluster", "annotation"), confirm = "yes") result$status ## [1] "completed" result$report$status ## [1] "completed" RunAIAnalysis() is one round: plan, validate, preview, ask, execute, and optionally interpret. Running it again is how you continue — there is no loop option to look for, for the reason given in the previous chapter: the engine executes one plan and never re-plans mid-run. result$status is the execution outcome; result$report$status is the planning outcome. They are different fields because they are different questions, and a plan can be fine while an execution fails. Passing confirm = "yes" executes without pausing, which is right for a script and wrong for exploratory use. Leave it out and read the preview first. 29.5 Free-form questions with sclet_copilot Not every question is a plan. sclet_copilot() answers a free-form question about an object by reading its recorded provenance — what analysis ran, in what order, with which parameters — instead of looking at the data alone. sclet_copilot(demo, "I clustered this object after normalization. What should I check before trusting the clusters?") ## [1] "Read-only status readout of the sclet dataset plus a proposed descriptive-spine plan; nothing was executed. The dataset is 200 cells x 60 genes with counts/logcounts/scaled layers, a 10-PC PCA, and a k=10 rank SNN graph (200 vertices / 9184 edges). The recorded chain (normalize_logcounts, pca, knn_graph, louvain_clusters) is completed. colLabels has 5 groups (46/47/45/46/16), all above the 10-cell aggregation threshold. No marker test, no trajectory, and no reference annotation have been run; velocity, differential abundance, spatial and multimodal questions are blocked by missing inputs/records. Proposed plan: (1) cluster-vs-rest marker test on logcounts, (2) Treatment contrast (cell-level only, no replicates), (3) optional trajectory ordering on PCA + colLabels, which is not a lineage claim." The value here is narrow and worth stating. The tool cannot see your cells; it can see what the ledger recorded and in which order. That is enough to discuss the workflow, and not enough to make a claim about the biology. 29.6 Cross-chain auditing AuditAnalysisChain() asks a narrower question: does the expression of specific genes look distorted by an earlier step? It traces the state machine back to the raw layer and compares. It needs an integration that produces a corrected expression layer. fastMNN does, but only when asked for full-gene output — by default it returns a corrected embedding and the logical corrected layer falls back to the source expression, which is not something to audit: demo <- RunIntegration(demo, method = "fastMNN", batch = "batch", correct.all = TRUE) # The logical layer is the vocabulary; the assay behind it is an implementation # detail that the audit resolves for you. SummarizedExperiment::assayNames(demo) ## [1] "counts" "logcounts" "scaled" ## [4] "reconstructed" audit <- AuditAnalysisChain( demo, features = head(rownames(demo), 5), raw_layer = "counts", integrated_layer = "corrected" ) cat(audit) ## The ledger establishes the object's structure (200 cells x 60 genes; assays counts/logcounts/scaled/reconstructed; layers counts/logcounts/scaled/corrected/reconstructed; 5 colLabels groups) and that of the five requested features only Gene_0003 is a selected HVG, while Gene_0001, Gene_0002, Gene_0004 and Gene_0005 are non-selected bystanders carried into `reconstructed` only under `correct.all = TRUE`. It does not establish whether the requested features agree between `counts` and `reconstructed`: no per-gene layer statistics are recorded, and no ai_evidence nodes exist in the supplied ledger. The chain also has structural problems that constrain interpretation: the HVG step requested n = 5000 on a 60-gene object and selected 29 genes without reconciliation; the knn_graph and Louvain clusters were built on uncorrected PCA (dims 1:10, layer `scaled`, integration = null) while the active reduction is the 28-component `corrected` embedding, so the clusters are not batch-corrected clusters; the corrected embedding has no recorded downstream use; integration has two records with a flagged conflict and fastmnn lineage parents are null; `counts` was never corrected and never used for the graph; design semantics (batch, Treatment) are unconfirmed; and there are no markers, trajectory or annotation. Verification is proposed as four steps: a layer-agreement check for Gene_0001-Gene_0005, re-deriving the graph on the corrected embedding, a marker test on the resulting clusters, and confirmation of design semantics before any condition contrast. What it returns matters more than what it prints. The results are recorded with claim levels, and the report’s own verification section re-derives them; a round that is not rendered loses that check. Audit output is input to a judgement, not the judgement. Be aware of which integration method you used: fastMNN produces a corrected expression layer (with correct.all = TRUE), so the comparison above is the right abstraction. Harmony and scVI produce a corrected reduction — no corrected expression exists to compare against, so this particular audit does not apply and needs adapting. 29.7 A plan does not replace the workflow functions RunBasicWorkflow(), RunStandardPipeline() and the other Run<Mainline>Workflow() shells are the way to run a whole mainline in one call, and they are not registry actions: a shell chains several actions, and a plan that used one would have a single opaque step where the engine wants inspectable ones. Plan the same work from the actions it is made of — that is what the trace records, step by step, and it is why a completed round can be read back as a graph rather than as one black box. 29.8 What the planner can and cannot see The in-package assistant plans against the same registry as everything else, but it is shown a subset: an action whose required input only a person can supply — a gene set, a bulk phenotype matrix, a reference object — is marked planner_visible = FALSE and stays out of its catalog. RunAIAnalysis() therefore covers the analyses whose inputs live on the object, and a goal that needs external material is a driver-mode job, covered in the driver chapter. That distinction is worth knowing before you blame the model. A goal about gene-set scoring is not a capability the assistant lacks; it is a goal it cannot plan, and the honest response is to say which input is missing rather than to propose a step that would fail validation. 29.9 What the package will not do It will not call a provider unless you ask for one explicitly; it will not present a claim stronger than its evidence supports; and it will not treat a successful plan as a successful analysis, because “all steps completed” and “the question was answered” are different statements. The last chapter covers how that difference is enforced.

30 Evidence Governance: Claims, Results, and Reports 30.1 Evidence nodes 30.2 The claim ceiling 30.3 What may leave the object: the privacy line 30.4 Recording results 30.5 RenderAIReport: the report checks itself 30.6 The failure this whole layer is against

30 Evidence Governance: Claims, Results, and Reports An analysis that runs is not an analysis that means anything. The first two chapters of this part get a plan executed; this one is about what may be said afterwards, and why sclet refuses to let you say more. The rule this chapter exists to enforce: a report may only claim what the evidence supports. Every other function in the AI layer is upstream of that check. 30.1 Evidence nodes An evidence node is a bounded, named record that something was measured. Two properties make it useful: It is aggregate by construction. Cell counts, gene counts, quantiles, booleans — never a feature name, an antibody name, a barcode, or a per-cell value. A complete matrix is rejected, not truncated. This is what makes a node safe to put in a prompt. It is write-once, unless the analysis says otherwise. Recording the same node id twice with identical values is a no-op; with different values it raises evidence_id_conflict rather than overwriting. A re-run that silently kept the first run’s numbers would be a citable artifact describing an older analysis — worse than a missing node, because it renders and looks like a measurement of the current object. The exception is the case where the analysis knows it is re-running itself under a fixed id — imputation is the example: its record id is the same on every run, and its action passes replace = TRUE so the node is refreshed in place. The rule is not “never overwrite” but “never overwrite silently”: an id that a caller cannot rename refreshes and the trace records it as such; an id a caller could have renamed must not. library(sclet) sce <- scuttle::mockSCE(ncells = 200, ngenes = 80) sce <- SingleCellExperiment::SingleCellExperiment( list(counts = SummarizedExperiment::assay(sce, "counts")) ) ev <- list( id = "ev:demo_doublet_finder", kind = "deterministic_summary", summary = list(n_cells = 200L, n_doublets = 12L) ) with_ev <- RecordAIEvidence(sce, ev) GetAnalysisLedger(with_ev)$analyses[grepl("demo", names(GetAnalysisLedger(with_ev)$analyses))] ## ## ## $`ai_evidence::ev:demo_doublet_finder`$created_at ## [1] "2026-10-22 14:51:42.152213" sclet_ai_record_evidence_for_run() is the recorder used inside sclet itself: it tolerates a re-run whose values are unchanged, and refuses one whose values changed unless asked with replace = TRUE. 30.2 The claim ceiling Every interpretive statement has a claim level, derived from the evidence behind it — not from the confidence of whoever wrote it. GetAnalysisLedger() carries the ceiling, and ValidateAIPlan() reports it alongside a plan. The clearest consequence: two evidence nodes that share a dependency group are not two lines of support. Run a second contrast over the same graph and you have a second analysis, not independent confirmation. sclet_ai_evidence_independence() answers that question structurally: a <- list(id = "ev:a", kind = "deterministic_summary", summary = list(n = 10L), dependency_group = "group_1") b <- list(id = "ev:b", kind = "deterministic_summary", summary = list(n = 10L), dependency_group = "group_1") sce_a <- RecordAIEvidence(sce, a) sce_ab <- RecordAIEvidence(sce_a, b) sclet_ai_evidence_independence(sce_ab, c("ev:a", "ev:b"))$independent ## [1] FALSE Common lineage is not a flaw to hide; it is a fact to report. A report that counts the same signal twice overstates its case, which is exactly the failure mode this layer exists for. 30.3 What may leave the object: the privacy line Design semantics may be exposed. Analysis results may not. The distinction is not “no colData values leave”, because a contrast cannot be planned without the levels of the design column. The line is about what the analysis is trying to discover: ActiveIdent — the clustering — is the result. It leaves only as group_N codes. Revealing cluster names pre-answers the question the analysis was asked. A design column — condition, Treatment, donor — is the user’s own experimental setup. Its levels must be present, or the planner has to invent them. capabilities$contrast_levels therefore lists design levels and must exclude the active identity column by name, while capabilities$identity_levels stays anonymised. Two traps found while implementing this: levels must be a character vector (an unnamed list of scalars is redacted as “unnamed nested values are not bounded”), and note is on the privacy deny list, so explanatory text belongs in guidance. 30.4 Recording results RecordAIResult() attaches an interpretive result to the object with its supporting evidence attached, so a result cannot be separated from what backs it. ValidateAIEvidenceRefs() checks references against the ledger and enforces the scope and cross-kind rules: a reference may not scope outside the supporting evidence’s own scope, and AI-generated claims may not cite user_decision nodes. 30.5 RenderAIReport: the report checks itself A round is not finished when execution returns. It is finished when the report has been rendered and its self-check agreed with the ledger. sce2 <- scuttle::mockSCE(ncells = 200, ngenes = 80) sce2 <- SingleCellExperiment::SingleCellExperiment( list(counts = SummarizedExperiment::assay(sce2, "counts")) ) # RunDEtest() needs an identity to test against, so go through the same short # preprocessing chain the driver chapter uses. `RunDEtest()` also refuses a # single-group object: a marker test on one cluster is undefined, not empty. sce2 <- NormalizeData(sce2) sce2 <- FindVariableFeatures(sce2) sce2 <- ScaleData(sce2) sce2 <- RunPCA(sce2, ncomponents = 10) sce2 <- FindNeighbors(sce2, dims = 1:10) sce2 <- FindClusters(sce2, resolution = 1.0) sce2 <- RunDEtest(sce2, only.pos = TRUE, name = "markers") ledger <- GetAnalysisLedger(sce2) nrow(ledger$analyses) ## NULL RenderAIReport() re-derives every recorded claim level from the evidence and re-resolves every citation, then prints any disagreement in its own verification section. A round that is not rendered loses that check — and the next round then plans from a raw record, which is where overstated claims get quietly carried forward. 30.6 The failure this whole layer is against Three failure modes are invisible without it: a silent no-op, where a recorder swallowed an error and the ledger kept the earlier run’s numbers; borrowed support, where two nodes from one analysis counted as independent confirmation; an unrendered round, where nothing re-derived the claims that were made. Each is a way for a document to say something stronger than the object it describes. The ledger, the ceiling, and the report are three views of the same defence.
